source_text:
Quamquam si philosophandi libido est, Socraten, sapientiae principem, quisque uestrum tantus est, si potuerit, imitetur. eius uiri, quotiens de caelestibus rogabatur, nota responsio est: quod supra nos, nihil ad nos.
merito ergo de oraculo testimonium meruit prudentiae singularis. quod oraculum, idem ipse persensit, idcirco uniuersis se esse praepositum, non quod omnia comperisset, sed quod nihil se scire didicisset: ita confessae inperitiae summa prudentia est.
hoc fonte defluxit Arcesilae et multo post Carneadis et Academicorum plurimorum in summis quaestionibus tuta dubitatio, quo genere philosophari et caute indocti. possunt et docti gloriose.
quid, Simonidis melici nonne admiranda omnibus et sectanda cunctatio? qui Simonides, cum de eo, quid et quales arbitraretur deos, ab Hierone tyranno quaereretur, primo deliberationi diem petiit, postridie biduum prorogauit, mox: alterum tantum admonitus adiunxit. postremo cum causas tantae morae tyrannus inquireret, respondit ille, quod sibi quanto inquisitio tardior pergeret, tanto ueritas fieret obscurior.
mea quoque opinione quae sunt dubia, ut sunt, relinquenda sunt, nec tot ac tantis uiris deliberantibus temere et audaciter in alteram partem ferenda sententia est, ne aut anilis inducatur superstitio aut omnis religio destruatur.
thought_title: Socratic ignorance as the model of cautious doubt
orientation: Caecilius is still speaking, arguing that human knowledge is uncertain and that the wisest course is to leave doubtful questions undecided.
pass_a_gloss: But if there is a desire to philosophize, let each of you who is so great imitate Socrates, the prince of wisdom, if he can. Of that man, whenever he was asked about heavenly things, the well-known answer is: what is above us, is nothing to us. Therefore he deservedly earned the testimony of singular prudence from the oracle. Which oracle, he himself perceived the same thing, that he was set before all men for this reason, not because he had found out all things, but because he had learned that he knew nothing: thus the highest prudence is confessed ignorance. From this source flowed the safe doubt of Arcesilaus and much later of Carneades and of very many Academics in the highest questions, by which kind of philosophizing both the unlearned can do so cautiously and the learned can do so gloriously. What, is not the admirable and to-be-followed hesitation of Simonides the lyric poet to be admired by all? Which Simonides, when he was asked by the tyrant Hiero what he thought the gods were and of what kind, first asked for a day for deliberation, the next day he put it off for two days, soon after, when reminded, he added another equal amount. Finally when the tyrant asked the causes of so great a delay, he answered that the slower the inquiry proceeded for him, the more obscure the truth became. In my opinion also, things which are doubtful, as they are, are to be left alone, nor is a judgment to be rashly and boldly brought to one side or the other by so many and such great men deliberating, lest either old-womanish superstition be introduced or all religion be destroyed.

choices.why: Keeps the honorific force of princeps as first or foremost, matching the Latin idiom.

choices.term: quod supra nos, nihil ad nos
choices.english: what is above us, is nothing to us
choices.why: Preserves the parallel structure and the blunt force of the Latin aphorism.
rejected: things above us do not concern us
what is beyond us is none of our business

choices.english: the highest prudence is confessed ignorance
choices.why: Keeps the paradox of confessed ignorance as the summit of prudence, with inperitia as ignorance.
rejected: the greatest wisdom is to admit ignorance
supreme wisdom is acknowledged lack of skill

choices.why: Renders tuta as safe, capturing the Academic suspension of judgment as a protective stance.
Keeps the dismissive gendered insult of anilis, matching the glossary term superstition.
Uses the glossary term religion for religio and keeps the strong verb destruatur.

pass_b_english: And yet, if you have a passion for philosophy, let any of you who is great enough imitate Socrates, the prince of wisdom, if you can. Whenever that man was asked about heavenly matters, his famous answer was: what is above us is nothing to us.

So he rightly earned from the oracle the testimony of singular prudence. He himself understood that oracle: he had been set above all men not because he had found out everything, but because he had learned that he knew nothing. Thus the highest prudence is confessed ignorance.

From this source flowed the safe doubt of Arcesilaus, and much later of Carneades and very many of the Academics, in the highest questions. It is a way of philosophizing in which the unlearned can proceed cautiously and the learned gloriously.

And what of Simonides the lyric poet? Is not his hesitation admirable to all and worthy of imitation? When the tyrant Hiero asked him what he thought the gods were and of what kind, Simonides first asked for a day to deliberate, the next day put it off for two more, and soon, when reminded, added another one. Finally, when the tyrant asked the reasons for such a long delay, he answered that the slower his inquiry proceeded, the more obscure the truth became.

In my opinion too, things that are doubtful should be left as they are, doubtful. And when so many and such great men are deliberating, one should not rashly and boldly cast a judgment for one side or the other, lest either old-womanish superstition be introduced or all religion be destroyed.

problems.why: Latin ‘si potuerit’ refers to the addressee’s ability, not Socrates’; English misattributes ability to Socrates.
problems.ruling: Latin 'quisque...si potuerit' = 'anyone of you if he is able'; 'potuerit' refers to the addressee's ability to imitate, not Socrates' ability.

problems.why: Latin says he added only one more (alterum), but English says two.
problems.ruling: Latin 'alterum tantum' = 'another of the same amount' (i.e., two more days, matching the prior 'biduum'); English 'another two' correctly renders this.

edits.old: imitate Socrates, the prince of wisdom, if he can.
edits.new: imitate Socrates, the prince of wisdom, if you can.

fixed: Agency: 'si potuerit' refers to the addressee's ability, not Socrates'; changed 'if he can' to 'if you can'.
Addition: 'alterum tantum' means one more equal amount, not two; changed 'added another two' to 'added another one'.

polish.changed: I broke the long paragraph into shorter paragraphs at natural turns in thought, clarified the implied subject of the Simonides anecdote, and smoothed sentence rhythm while preserving every claim, qualification, and quotation exactly.

notes.why: Arcesilaus is a specific Hellenistic philosopher associated with Academic skepticism, unexplained here.
notes.fix: Identify Arcesilaus as a leader of the skeptical Academy.

notes.quote: my friend Natalis's opinion has wavered
notes.why: Caecilius is suddenly called 'Natalis' with no explanation; reader thinks a new person.
notes.fix: Add note: Natalis is an alternate name for Caecilius.

notes.quote: the safe doubt of Arcesilaus, and much later of Carneades and very many of the Academics
notes.fix: Note: Arcesilaus and Carneades led the skeptical Academy.

notes.why: Hiero, tyrant of Syracuse, is cited without context.
notes.fix: Note: Hiero was tyrant of Syracuse (5th c. BC).
